```{python}
#| label: setup-disc

import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
ARMS = (("ISLA", "isla", "isla_ref"), ("GeoTransolver", "gt_unit", "gt"), ("Transolver", "transolver_unit", "t"))
# the inference-draw probes and the training-law swap: DrivAerML Surface task (435 cars, 100,000 cells) and the 35-wing rung (200,000 cells).
# ISLA rows are the reference configuration R1 (REF-BOARD inference half, 2026-09-23); the baselines are the released
# checkpoints of the training-law study (cars) and the 200k fleet (wings), probed under the same draws.
TC = J("trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json"); TW = J("trainarea_reduction_2026-09-20.json")
WB = J("wingbench_200k_reduction_2026-09-19.json")["arms"]
CR = J("consistency_r1_2026-09-23.json")["arms"]
DENS = {"DrivAerML Surface task, 435 training cars, 100,000 cells": {"isla": CR["isla_r1_dr435_100k"], "gt_unit": TC["arms"]["gt_unit_uniform"], "transolver_unit": TC["arms"]["transolver_unit_uniform"]},
        "HiLiftAeroML, 35 training cases, 200,000 cells": {"isla": CR["isla_r1_hl35_200k"], "gt_unit": WB["gt_unit_lr3e3"], "transolver_unit": WB["transolver_unit"]}}
CR200 = CR["isla_r1_dr435_200k"]
factor = lambda a, draw="biased": a["mean"][draw] / a["mean"]["unif"]
seed_factors = lambda a, draw="biased": [s[draw] / s["unif"] for s in a["per_seed"].values()]
# slice territories on both datasets (ISLA R1 against the released GeoTransolver-256), and pose at the reporting protocol
TT = J("territory_r1_2026-09-23.json")["models"]; TTW = J("territory_wings_r1_2026-09-23.json")["models"]; TT200 = J("territory_r1_200k_2026-09-23.json")["models"]
POSE = J("p200k_pose_r1_2026-09-23.json"); PA, PV, PN = POSE["arms"], POSE["verdict"], POSE["native_frame_reference"]
```

## Sampling-density robustness {#sec-robustness-density}


```{python}
#| label: para-density-lede
#| output: asis
dc, dw = DENS["DrivAerML Surface task, 435 training cars, 100,000 cells"], DENS["HiLiftAeroML, 35 training cases, 200,000 cells"]
smax = max(abs(1 - factor(a, "strat")) for d in DENS.values() for a in d.values())
print(f"**Under a 10:1 spatially biased sampling density at inference ISLA's error grows by {(factor(dc['isla']) - 1) * 100:.0f}% on the cars at "
      f"100,000 cells and by {(factor(CR200) - 1) * 100:.0f}% at its 200,000-cell protocol, and is unchanged on the wings. GeoTransolver's and "
      "Transolver's, which center their coordinates on the sampled points, grow by factors.** The probe evaluates a trained model on its "
      "validation surfaces with cells drawn ten times more densely at the front of the body than at the back (the third draw of "
      "@sec-sampling-laws), with exact Horvitz–Thompson measure weights so that every weighted integral is unbiased. The readout is the "
      "error under the biased draw divided by the same checkpoint's error under an independent uniform draw at the same count. A ratio of 1 "
      "means the prediction depends only on the surface and not on how it was sampled. Every ratio here is in the *sample frame*: each "
      "model's coordinates are centered on the biased sample itself, which is what a biased mesher delivers and what ISLA computes inside "
      "the model. The stratified draw, which keeps the sampling law and only spreads the cells, is the control. It moves no model by more "
      f"than {smax * 100:.1f}% (and only ever downward), so the biased column measures the law and not draw-to-draw noise.")
```

The mechanism is the one @sec-isla-frame teaches. ISLA has no origin.
Its translation invariance comes from point-to-anchor differences, and its
length unit is a measure-weighted integral of the sampled surface that the
biased draw estimates without bias. GeoTransolver and Transolver consume
coordinates that the datapipe centers on the plain mean of the sampled
points. That mean moves by 0.94 RMS radii under the 10:1 bias on the cars,
and every downstream quantity moves with it.


Two things follow. The sensitivity is the **frame, not the aggregation**.
GeoTransolver given ISLA's measure-weighted pooling (an ablation, not a
modification of the public model, @sec-part-baseline) keeps its factor.
Given in addition a datapipe centered on the Horvitz–Thompson centroid, it
comes close to one (@sec-nb-steelman-verdict; @tbl-consistency-40k carries
the pooling ablation). What those ablations buy consistency with is a body
centroid, a point the physics does not distinguish and that is ill-posed
for an open, truncated or multi-body boundary, and they remain
non-covariant. The comparison the book makes is "consistent and exactly
covariant without any centroid" against "consistent with a centroid, not
covariant" (@sec-isla-variants). ISLA's residual is the **variance of its
measure-weighted routing integral** under a 10:1 sample, not a frame
effect, and it shrinks with the cell count as quadrature error does. On
the cars the same reference-configuration checkpoint reads 1.10x at
100,000 cells and 1.01x at 200,000, where the sparse half of the biased
draw still holds tens of thousands of cells. On the wings, whose
200,000-cell draws are the only ones run, nothing is measurable.

## Consistency under refinement and across samplers {#sec-consistency-bench}

**No configuration gives the same field under a different sampling of the
same surface at 10,000 cells. ISLA's relative frame converges toward it as
the sample grows, and GeoTransolver and Transolver do not.** The benchmark
is a mechanism diagnostic, not a standing. It runs on exploration-budget
checkpoints (trained at 10,000 cells per case) evaluated at 2,500 to 40,000
cells, and no accuracy is read from it. It asks the question the principle
of @sec-discretization-centerpiece poses: does a model converge to one
field under refinement, and to the same field under two sampling laws?
Every checkpoint is evaluated in float32 on the same validation surfaces
sampled three ways from a 320,000-cell pool: uniformly over cells (the
training convention, which inherits the mesher's refinement),
proportionally to cell area (the law of a uniform point-cloud generator),
and with the 10:1 bias. Each draw carries exact Horvitz–Thompson weights,
so a measure-consistent model sees the same integral under all three.

```{python}
#| label: fig-consistency-curves
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Convergence toward consistency. Each panel plots an architecture's
#|   surface-pressure error divided by the same architecture's error under
#|   uniform sampling at 40,000 cells, against the number of sampled cells,
#|   for three samplers (columns) and two validation sets (rows); a curve
#|   approaching 1 converges to the uniform-sampling answer. Uniform sampling
#|   (left) converges for every arm. Under the area-proportional sampler
#|   (middle) the ISLA curves fall toward 1 while the baselines are flat.
#|   Under the 10:1 bias (right) the ISLA curves approach the uniform answer
#|   at 40,000 cells. ISLA was benchmarked from 10,000 cells, so its curves
#|   start there. How to read this: only the trend with count is
#|   interpretable under the area sampler, whose weights span four decades
#|   and leave refined regions unsampled at small counts, so fixed-count
#|   values there mix information loss with model dependence; the
#|   checkpoints are exploration-budget lanes, so no panel is an accuracy
#|   standing. Seed means over two seeds; float32. Data:
#|   results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json,

A = dict(B["arms"]); COUNTS = [str(c) for c in B["counts"]]
A.update(json.load(open(RES / "consistency_bench" / "consistency_bench_rf_2026-09-11.json"))["arms"])
ROWS = [
 ("DrivAerML, 48 cars", {"isla_ref": "rf_dr_mt2_meas", "gt": "uw_gt_unit_lr1e3", "t": "uw_transolver_unit_lr3e3"}),
 ("HiLift, 35 training cases", {"isla_ref": "rf_hl_mt2_meas_super_scarce", "gt": "udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3", "t": "udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3"}),
]
SAMPLERS = [("unif", "uniform over cells"), ("area", "area-proportional"), ("biased", "10:1 front/back bias")]
def err(arm, sampler, count):

fig, axs = plt.subplots(len(ROWS), 3, figsize=(10.2, 6.6), sharex=True)

        ax = axs[i, j]

            ax.plot([int(c) for c in counts], y, **series_kwargs(key, lw=1.6, ms=5, label=(STYLE[key]["label"] if (i == 0 and j == 0) else None)), zorder=3)
        ax.axhline(1.0, color=BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)

        ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(["2.5k", "5k", "10k", "20k", "40k"]); ax.set_xlim(2100, 4.8e4)

        if i == len(ROWS) - 1: ax.set_xlabel("sampled cells per case [count]")
handles, labels_ = axs[0, 0].get_legend_handles_labels()
fig.legend(handles, labels_, loc="upper left", ncol=4, fontsize=8.5, bbox_to_anchor=(0.01, 0.99), handlelength=2.4, columnspacing=1.4)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.93))
```

## The law the training sample is drawn by: two datasets {#sec-training-law}


**A GeoTransolver or Transolver checkpoint is accurate on the sampling law
it was trained under and on no other. ISLA's trained function is weakly
dependent on the law.** Changing the draw at inference is one half of the
discretization question. Changing the law the model is *trained* under is
the other half, and it is the half a practitioner meets when a surrogate
trained on one mesher's output is handed a mesh from another. On each
dataset the three models are trained twice: under the uniform-over-cells
law and under the area-proportional Poisson law of @sec-sampling-laws with
exact Horvitz–Thompson weights. Every checkpoint is scored on the same
validation surfaces under the same independent uniform draw (float32, two
seeds; 35 wings at 200,000 cells per case, 435 cars at 100,000).

```{python}
        ax.plot([k], [u], marker=kw["marker"], color=kw["color"], mfc=kw["color"], mec=kw["color"], ls="none", ms=9, zorder=4)
        ax.plot([k], [a], marker=kw["marker"], color=kw["color"], mfc="white", mec=kw["color"], mew=1.8, ls="none", ms=9, zorder=4)
        ax.plot([k] * 2, us, ls="none", marker="o", color=kw["color"], ms=3.5, zorder=5); ax.plot([k] * 2, as_, ls="none", marker="o", color=kw["color"], ms=3.5, zorder=5)
        ax.text(k + 0.1, (u * a) ** 0.5, f"×{a / u:.2f}" if a / u < 2 else f"×{a / u:.1f}", color=kw["color"], fontsize=9.5, va="center", path_effects=halo())
    ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xticks([0, 1, 2]); ax.set_xticklabels([a_[0] for a_ in ARMS])
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:g}")); ax.yaxis.set_minor_formatter(mpl.ticker.NullFormatter())
    ax.set_yticks([0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5]); ax.set_ylim(0.035, 0.6); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 2.6)
    ax.set_title(title + ", scored on the independent uniform draw", fontsize=9.5); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.set_ylabel("surface-pressure relative L2 error [–]")
h = [mpl.lines.Line2D([], [], marker="o", color=INK2, ls="none", ms=8, label="trained under the uniform-over-cells law (filled)"),
     mpl.lines.Line2D([], [], marker="o", color=INK2, mfc="white", mew=1.8, ls="none", ms=8, label="the same configuration trained under the area-proportional law (open)"),
     mpl.lines.Line2D([], [], marker="o", color=INK2, ls="none", ms=3.5, label="seeds (dots)")]
fig2.legend(handles=h, loc="upper left", ncol=3, fontsize=8.5, bbox_to_anchor=(0.01, 1.0))
fig2.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.93))
plt.show()
```

```{python}
def paired(arms, m):
    su = arms[f"{m}_uniform"]["per_seed"]; sa = arms[f"{m}_area"]["per_seed"]
    return [sa[s]["unif"] / su[s]["unif"] for s in su]
out = "| model | HiLiftAeroML, 35 training cases, 200,000 cells | DrivAerML Surface task, 435 training cars, 100,000 cells |\n|---|---:|---:|\n"
for label, m, _ in ARMS:
    pw, pc = paired(W, m), paired(C, m)
    out += f"| {label} | {TW['verdict'][f'{m}_area_over_uniform_unif']:.2f}x ({min(pw):.2f}–{max(pw):.2f}) | {TC['verdict'][f'{m}_area_over_uniform_unif']:.2f}x ({min(pc):.2f}–{max(pc):.2f}) |\n"
print(out)
print(": The training-law change on two datasets: surface-pressure error of the checkpoint trained under the area-proportional Poisson law "
      "divided by that of the same configuration trained under the uniform-over-cells law, both scored on the same validation surfaces under "
      "the independent uniform draw (float32, seed means; in parentheses the range of the seed-paired ratios; each architecture at its "
      "reporting-protocol rate). How to read this: 1 means the trained function does not depend on the law its training sample was drawn by. "
      "Data: results/trainarea_reduction_2026-09-20.json; results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json. {#tbl-scoreboard-training-law}")
```

```{python}
#| label: para-training-law
#| output: asis
def r(arms, m): return arms[f"{m}_area"]["mean"]["unif"] / arms[f"{m}_uniform"]["mean"]["unif"]
print(f"On the wings ISLA's error moves from {W['isla_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f} to {W['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.4f} ({r(W,'isla'):.2f}x), "
      f"GeoTransolver's from {W['gt_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f} to {W['gt_unit_area']['mean']['unif']:.4f} ({r(W,'gt_unit'):.1f}x) and Transolver's from "
      f"{W['transolver_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f} to {W['transolver_unit_area']['mean']['unif']:.4f} ({r(W,'transolver_unit'):.1f}x). "
      f"On the cars the same swap moves ISLA from {C['isla_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f} to {C['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.4f} ({r(C,'isla'):.2f}x), "
      f"GeoTransolver from {C['gt_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f} to {C['gt_unit_area']['mean']['unif']:.3f} ({r(C,'gt_unit'):.1f}x) and Transolver from "
      f"{C['transolver_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f} to {C['transolver_unit_area']['mean']['unif']:.3f} ({r(C,'transolver_unit'):.1f}x), errors close to that of predicting the mean field. "
      f"Under the area law ISLA leads GeoTransolver and Transolver on the uniform draw by {W['gt_unit_area']['mean']['unif']/W['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.1f}x and {W['transolver_unit_area']['mean']['unif']/W['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.1f}x on the wings and by "
      f"{C['gt_unit_area']['mean']['unif']/C['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.1f}x and {C['transolver_unit_area']['mean']['unif']/C['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.1f}x on the cars. Under the uniform law it trails them by "
      f"{(1 - W['gt_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']/W['isla_uniform']['mean']['unif'])*100:.0f}% on the wings and is at parity on the cars (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA {C['gt_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']/C['isla_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.2f}). "
      "This is the one setting on the wings in which ISLA's lead is a factor rather than a percentage.")
```

The mechanism is the one @sec-isla-quadrature teaches. The baselines' slice
aggregates are averages over the kept points, so the trained function
absorbs the point pattern it was fitted on and is wrong on any other.
ISLA's aggregates are measure-weighted integrals, the same under any draw
that carries its weights. @sec-territories looks at this directly in the
two trained networks. Two qualifications travel with the figure. First,
ISLA is not indifferent. Its 8% on the cars for the 192-wide lanes of the
table, and 5% for the reference configuration re-run at 200,000 cells
(seeds 4% and 6%; @sec-nb-refboard-area-twin,
results/trainarea_dr_r1_2026-09-23.json), sit at or past the 5% bar the
DrivAerML twin preregistered (@sec-nb-trainarea-dr-verdict). The statement
is therefore "weakly dependent" beside baselines that are dependent by
factors of 2.4 to 9.6. Part of the few percent is the quadrature noise of
an area-proportional draw whose weights span four decades on these meshes
(@fig-consistency-curves). Second, the baselines' dependence is much
larger on the cars than on the wings, although the cars' cell-area spread
is the smaller (coefficient of variation 2.3 against 3.3). The cell-area
spread alone does not explain this, and it is an open question
(@sec-open-questions).

## Where the slices sit: territories under a change of draw {#sec-territories}

```{python}
#| label: para-territory-lede
#| output: asis
I, G = TT["ISLA"]["summary"], TT["GeoTransolver"]["summary"]; I43 = TT["ISLA_seed43"]["summary"]
IW, GW = TTW["ISLA"]["summary"], TTW["GeoTransolver"]["summary"]; IW43 = TTW["ISLA_seed43"]["summary"]
print(f"**GeoTransolver's slices follow the points and ISLA's nearly do not. On the cars, under the 10:1-biased draw GeoTransolver's slice "
      f"territories lose a third of their agreement with the uniform draw beyond what a fresh uniform draw costs, and its slice centroids move "
      f"by {G['displacement_median']:.1f} of the body's radius. ISLA loses {I['excess_median']:.2f}, and its anchors move by "
      f"{I['displacement_median']:.2f}. On the wings the centroids move {GW['displacement_median']:.1f} and the anchors "
      f"{IW['displacement_median']:.3f}.** The mechanism above is argued from the equations. The probe here looks at the routing of the "
      "uniform-trained checkpoints (ISLA at the reference configuration, two seeds; GeoTransolver-256; the cars probed at 100,000 cells, "
      "the 35-wing rung at 200,000) on four validation cases under three independent draws of the same surface: two uniform draws and the "
      "10:1-biased draw of @sec-sampling-laws. For every token the probe records its **dominant slice** in each block (the slice with the "
      "largest read-back weight for ISLA, the largest slice weight for GeoTransolver). It then matches every token of one draw to its nearest token "
      "of another on the surface and counts how often the dominant slice agrees. Two uniform draws set the **resampling floor**: soft "
      "boundaries move a little under any resampling, so the floor is below one. The **bias excess** is how much further the agreement "
      "falls when the second draw is the biased one. The **anchor displacement** is the RMS motion of a slice's anchor (ISLA) or "
      "weight-averaged centroid (GeoTransolver) between the uniform and the biased draw, in units of the body's RMS radius. Its own "
      "floor is the same motion between the two uniform draws.")
```

```{python}
      "agreement columns there measure the softness of the routing and not its dependence on the draw. Weighting each slice by the tokens "
      "it owns instead of counting every slice once changes each displacement by 10% or less and no ordering (@sec-nb-territory-massweighted; "
      "results/territory_massweighted_2026-09-23.json). Data: "
      "results/territory_r1_2026-09-23.json; results/territory_r1_200k_2026-09-23.json; results/territory_wings_r1_2026-09-23.json. "
```

```{python}
      f"Second, the anchors' motion under the reference configuration ({I['displacement_median']:.2f} to {I43['displacement_median']:.2f} radii at 100,000 cells, {I200['displacement_median']:.2f} at "
```


```{python}
#| label: para-pose-canonical
#| output: asis
print("A GeoTransolver trained in a canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at about a percent of in-distribution accuracy "
      "(@sec-pose). What ISLA's construction buys is generality: it needs no known global direction to canonicalize against and no "
      "sign-resolvable principal frame. Where those fail, on a geometry with a degenerate inertia tensor or in a setting without a global "
      f"direction, the canonicalized model has no frame to compute, the augmented model pays the {(PA['gt_unit']['posed_over_native']-1)*100:.0f} to "
      f"{(PA['transolver_unit']['posed_over_native']-1)*100:.0f}% above, and the equivariant one is unaffected. The covariance is exact by "
      "algebraic construction and holds to roundoff in float64. On the trained GPU path it holds to 3e-5 in float32 and to about 4% "
      "under bf16 autocast, so the contract is exercised at deployment under float32 inference (@sec-isla-contracts).")
```
